patient.name: Joseph Mensah
patient.complaint: Fever, shaking and new confusion since last night
background: Long-term urinary catheter for urinary retention (enlarged prostate)
Type 2 diabetes on metformin and gliclazide
Lives with his wife in Croydon; no known drug allergies

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with fever (or hypothermia), tachycardia, hypotension and confusion after an infection, often in an older or immunosuppressed patient; septic shock if hypotension persists despite fluids.

points: Since last night: fever, rigors and cloudy, smelly urine in the bag.
His wife says he is **muddled** and not himself.
He is clammy and breathing fast.

steps.lead: Joseph has an infection (catheter urine) and his organs are struggling: confusion, low BP. That dysregulated response is **sepsis**.
Joseph's catheter infection is the key risk factor; his age, diabetes and kidney disease (chronic disease) add to it.
Joseph shows fever, tachycardia, **hypotension** and **altered mental state**: the typical presentation of sepsis.

visual.title: Joseph's heart rate against the high-risk cut-off
visual.label: Joseph 128
visual.caption: HR above **131** is a high-risk criterion. Joseph is just under, but his **BP under 90** and **RR over 25** already meet high-risk criteria.

steps.title: High-risk criteria: does Joseph meet them?
head: Criterion
Cut-off
Joseph
rows: Responds only to voice or pain, or unresponsive

steps.q: Joseph has a catheter infection, fever, confusion and BP 86/50 mmHg. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: Infection plus organ dysfunction (hypotension, confusion) = **sepsis**. Confusion here is a sign of hypoperfusion, not a separate diagnosis.

points: He receives two 500 mL fluid boluses over the next hour.
BP stays at **80/46 mmHg**; urine output under 10 mL/h.

steps.lead: Hypotension and low urine output persist **despite adequate fluids**: Joseph's sepsis has become **septic shock**.

steps.title: Infection to septic shock
steps.caption: Septic shock needs **vasopressors**; fluids alone will not fix it.

steps.text: Sepsis can present with **hypothermia**, not fever, especially in the elderly or immunosuppressed. A low temperature does not exclude it.
Classic stem: older patient, infection source, **fever or hypothermia**, tachycardia, hypotension and new confusion. Persistent low BP after fluids = **septic shock**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' with **blood cultures before antibiotics** or **lactate** as the answer, and septic-screen questions to find the source.

steps.lead: No single test proves sepsis. Joseph's diagnosis is **clinical**, and his **lactate** shows how severe it is.

points: Full observations and examination: warm peripheries, suprapubic tenderness.
Blood cultures taken **before** the first antibiotic dose.

steps.lead: Joseph's first-line set: vital signs, examination, **lactate**, FBC, U&Es, CRP, **blood cultures before antibiotics** and a blood gas.

steps.title: Joseph's first bloods
steps.text: High lactate (hypoperfusion), acidosis, raised inflammatory markers and **low albumin** from the acute-phase response.

visual.title: Joseph's lactate
visual.label: Joseph 4.6
visual.caption: Raised lactate = **hypoperfusion**. Above 4 is high risk; repeat it to track response.

steps.q: Joseph's antibiotics are drawn up. What must be done first, if it will not delay them?
steps.r: **Blood cultures before antibiotics**, because antibiotics may make cultures negative. Never delay antibiotics beyond the hour for them.

steps.lead: Joseph's septic screen: **catheter urine culture** (change the catheter first), chest X-ray to exclude a chest source, and a catheter for accurate input-output.

visual.title: Chest X-ray (septic screen)
visual.caption: Clear lungs: no pneumonia. The source is the **urine**, so the urine culture matters most.

steps.text: Do not wait for culture results, imaging or a CRP before giving antibiotics. Sepsis is diagnosed **clinically**; tests support it.
Lactate is the critical blood test: it shows **hypoperfusion** and its trend shows whether resuscitation is working.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (the Sepsis Six within 1 hour; IV antibiotics; 500 mL 0.9% saline bolus) and 'next step' after fluids fail (noradrenaline in ICU) or source control.

steps.title: Sepsis Six: within 1 hour
steps.caption: Three in (oxygen, antibiotics, fluids), three out (cultures, lactate, urine).

steps.lead: Joseph gets the **Sepsis Six** within the hour. Of all six, the **antibiotics** matter most.
ABCDE first, then a **500 mL 0.9% saline** bolus, cultures, and IV **piperacillin-tazobactam** (with metronidazole per local policy) within 1 hour.

steps.q: Joseph is hypotensive with suspected sepsis. Which IV fluid bolus is given first?
steps.r: A **500 mL crystalloid** (0.9% saline) bolus, then reassess. Glucose does not stay in the circulation; blood is for bleeding.

visual.title: Joseph's BP response
visual.caption: No response to fluids, so **septic shock**. MAP rises above **65** only once noradrenaline starts.

steps.lead: Joseph's BP did not respond to fluids, so ICU starts **noradrenaline**. Vasopressin or adrenaline would be added if it were not enough.

steps.q: After 1 L of fluid Joseph's MAP is 57 mmHg. Which is the next most appropriate step?
steps.r: Persistent hypotension despite fluids: contact ICU for a **noradrenaline infusion**.

points: Urine culture grows **E. coli** sensitive to the antibiotic.
Old catheter removed and replaced; antibiotics narrowed to the sensitivities.

steps.lead: The infected catheter is Joseph's source, so **removing it** is source control. An abscess would need draining.
Joseph's care follows **NICE NG51** for recognition and early management, and the UK Sepsis Trust's **Sepsis Six** bundle.

steps.text: Do not delay antibiotics to get blood cultures. Take cultures first **only if it does not delay** antibiotics beyond 1 hour.
Broad-spectrum first (Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobes), then **narrow once culture results** are back.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: why sepsis causes hypotension (cytokine vasodilation, capillary leak), why lactate rises, why albumin falls, or why vasopressors are needed.

steps.lead: Joseph's immune response to E. coli overshot: **TNF-alpha** and **IL-6** flooded his circulation.

steps.title: Why Joseph became hypotensive
nodes: Low BP and poor tissue perfusion

steps.lead: Joseph's tissues were short of oxygen, so cells switched to **anaerobic metabolism**, making the lactate of 4.6.

o: Anaerobic metabolism from poor tissue oxygen delivery
steps.r: Vasodilation and capillary leak reduce oxygen delivery, so cells make energy **anaerobically**, producing lactate.

steps.lead: Joseph's albumin of 27 reflects the **acute-phase response**: his liver is making CRP instead of albumin.
Vasodilation and a depressed heart overwhelmed Joseph's circulation despite fluids, so **noradrenaline** was needed to restore vascular tone.

steps.text: Exam phrase: hypotension in sepsis is caused by **cytokine-mediated vasodilation and capillary leak**, not by blood loss.

o: Life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to infection
mcq.r: Sepsis is a **dysregulated host response** to infection causing organ dysfunction.
**Septic shock**: sepsis with hypotension (and low urine output) despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

mcq.q: Which respiratory rate is a high-risk criterion in sepsis?
mcq.r: RR **>25/min** is high risk, along with systolic BP <90 and HR >131.

mcq.q: What is the gold standard for diagnosing sepsis?
mcq.r: Sepsis is a **clinical diagnosis plus lactate**.

mcq.q: What should be taken before antibiotics in sepsis, if possible?
mcq.r: **Blood cultures**, as antibiotics may alter culture results.

mcq.q: Within what time should the Sepsis Six be completed?
What is the single most important treatment for sepsis?
mcq.r: **Antibiotics** are the single most important treatment.

mcq.q: Which vasopressor is used first for hypotension unresponsive to fluids?
mcq.r: **Noradrenaline**, supplemented by vasopressin and adrenaline if needed.

mcq.q: Why is albumin often low in sepsis?
o: Liver makes inflammatory proteins instead of albumin
mcq.r: The liver's **acute-phase response** favours CRP and other inflammatory proteins over albumin.

mcq.q: Which cytokines drive vasodilation and capillary leak in sepsis?

technique.stem: A 74 year old woman has a 2 day history of productive cough and breathlessness. Today she is confused. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 122 bpm, BP 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. Her usual BP is 145/80 mmHg. There are coarse crackles at the right base.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question: infection signs plus organ dysfunction point one way.

clues: coarse crackles at the right base
steps.x: Pneumonia source, fever, hypotension (a 57 mmHg fall), RR over 25, new confusion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Infection plus organ dysfunction: **sepsis** from pneumonia.

elim: Heart failure gives bilateral crackles and oedema, not fever and a high CRP.
No allergen, urticaria or wheeze.
PE does not give a productive cough, fever and focal crackles.
Stroke does not explain fever, hypotension and a chest source.

steps.x: **D. Sepsis.** Infection + hypotension + confusion = sepsis.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man has fever, rigors and right loin pain. His temperature is 39.5°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 92/58 mmHg and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. He has been given oxygen and a cannula is in place. IV antibiotics are being prepared and can be given within 10 minutes.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation before the antibiotics are given?

steps.x: The test to do **before** antibiotics in suspected sepsis.

clues: fever, rigors and right loin pain
steps.x: Septic pyelonephritis; antibiotics imminent, so there is time for cultures without delay.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Blood cultures** before antibiotics, as antibiotics may alter the results.

elim: CT can come later to look for obstruction; it is not urgent before antibiotics.
Procalcitonin is not part of the first-line set and does not change immediate care.
Ultrasound helps find obstruction later, not before antibiotics.
A dipstick adds little; a urine culture matters more, and antibiotics only alter cultures.

steps.x: **A. Blood cultures.** Cultures first, but never delay antibiotics past 1 hour.

technique.stem: A 52 year old woman has cellulitis of the right leg and is now drowsy. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Her airway is patent. Two cannulas have been inserted and blood cultures taken.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial fluid management?
o: Maintenance fluid at 80 mL per hour
No fluid until the lactate is known

steps.x: Fluid choice and speed for a hypotensive septic patient.
Septic, hypotensive, access ready: give a fluid challenge now.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **500 mL 0.9% saline bolus**, then reassess.

elim: Glucose does not stay intravascular and slow fluid is useless in shock.
Albumin is not first-line resuscitation fluid.
Maintenance rate is far too slow for shock.
Never delay fluids for a result.

steps.x: **B. 500 mL 0.9% saline.** Bolus, reassess, repeat; vasopressors if it fails.

technique.stem: A 70 year old man is admitted with sepsis from a perforated appendix. His pulse rate is 116 bpm and BP 90/56 mmHg. He has no history of liver disease and ate normally until 2 days ago. His blood tests show CRP 290 mg/L and albumin 24 g/L.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his low albumin?
o: Hepatic synthesis diverted to acute-phase proteins
Loss of albumin in the stool

steps.x: Mechanism: why is albumin low in sepsis?
High CRP, low albumin, normal liver and diet.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The liver's **acute-phase response** makes CRP at the expense of albumin.

elim: Protein-losing enteropathy is chronic, not 2 days.
Two days of poor intake cannot drop albumin this much.
No proteinuria or oedema is described.
He has no liver disease and a normal ALT.

steps.x: **A. Acute-phase diversion.** Low albumin is a further sign of sepsis.

practice.stem: An 82 year old woman from a care home has become confused and is eating poorly. Staff say her urine has been offensive for 2 days. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 116 bpm, BP 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Her usual BP is 150/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A urinary source with fever, tachycardia, hypotension (a 62 mmHg fall) and new confusion is sepsis. Uncomplicated cystitis would not cause organ dysfunction.

steps.x: Most likely diagnosis in a confused, unwell older woman.
Urinary infection with fever, hypotension and altered mental state.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Infection plus organ dysfunction: **sepsis** (urinary source).

elim: Dementia is gradual and does not cause fever or hypotension.
Hypoglycaemia does not explain fever and a raised lactate.
Subdural gives fluctuating confusion after a fall, not fever.
Cystitis alone does not cause hypotension or confusion.

steps.x: **C. Sepsis.** New confusion is organ dysfunction, not just a UTI.

practice.stem: A 60 year old man with sepsis from cholangitis has received 2 L of IV crystalloid over 1 hour. His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 126 bpm and BP 78/44 mmHg (mean arterial pressure 55 mmHg). His urine output is 8 mL per hour. His jugular venous pressure is not raised and his peripheries are warm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Sepsis with persistent hypotension and low urine output despite adequate fluids is septic shock. Warm peripheries reflect vasodilation; hypovolaemic shock would respond to fluid.

steps.x: Which type of shock?
Known sepsis, hypotension persisting after fluid, warm vasodilated periphery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Septic shock**: hypotension despite adequate fluids.

elim: No allergen, rash or wheeze.
JVP not raised; no cardiac cause.
Hypovolaemia would respond to 2 L and gives cold peripheries.
No spinal injury; neurogenic shock gives bradycardia.

steps.x: **E. Septic shock.** Fluids given, BP still low.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman is admitted with sepsis from pneumonia. She has no history of liver or kidney disease and was eating well until 3 days ago. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. Her CRP is 260 mg/L.
practice.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on her blood tests?
practice.e: In sepsis the liver's acute-phase response favours inflammatory markers over albumin, so low albumin is a further sign.

steps.x: Predict a blood result in sepsis.

clues: no history of liver or kidney disease
steps.x: Strong acute-phase response; no other reason for abnormal proteins.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Low albumin**, from acute-phase diversion.

elim: Albumin falls, not rises, in sepsis.
Platelets may rise or fall but not above 1000.
CRP is already given as high.
Lactate is usually raised, not low.

steps.x: **C. Low albumin.** Liver makes CRP instead of albumin.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man has a 1 day history of fever and dysuria. He is alert and talking normally. His temperature is 38.7°C, oxygen saturation 96% breathing air and BP 128/76 mmHg, which is his usual. The doctor is deciding whether he meets any high-risk criteria for sepsis.
practice.q: Which additional finding would be a high-risk criterion for sepsis?
practice.e: High-risk criteria include RR over 25, systolic BP under 90 (or a fall over 40), MAP under 65, HR over 131 and reduced responsiveness. RR 27 meets one.

steps.x: Which number crosses a high-risk cut-off?

clues: BP 128/76 mmHg, which is his usual
steps.x: Infection, no organ dysfunction yet; look for the value beyond the threshold.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: RR **over 25**, HR over 131, systolic under 90, MAP under 65.

elim: 104 is raised but under 131.
112 is above 90 and only a 16 mmHg fall.
Fever is not itself a high-risk criterion.
Normal urine output.

steps.x: **B. RR 27.** Over 25 = high risk.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman with rheumatoid arthritis takes methotrexate and prednisolone. She has a 2 day history of feeling unwell, shivering and confusion after a dental abscess. Her temperature is 35.4°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 82/48 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Immunosuppression is a key risk factor; sepsis can cause hypothermia rather than fever. An infection source, tachycardia, hypotension and raised lactate confirm it.

steps.x: Diagnosis in an immunosuppressed, shocked patient.
Immunosuppressed, infection source, **hypothermia**, hypotension, confusion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sepsis**, presenting with hypothermia.

elim: Steroid use raises this risk, but the abscess, CRP 198 and lactate point to infection.
Hypothyroid coma gives bradycardia, not tachycardia.
Methotrexate toxicity gives mucositis and cytopenias, not this picture.
A flare causes joint pain, not shock.

steps.x: **E. Sepsis.** A low temperature does not exclude it.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman has a 3 day history of fever and right loin pain. She is drowsy and responds only to voice. Her temperature is 39.6°C, pulse rate 134 bpm, BP 84/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. Urine dipstick shows leucocytes and nitrites.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fever, loin pain and a positive dipstick with hypotension, HR over 131, RR over 25 and reduced responsiveness: high-risk sepsis from a urinary source.

steps.x: Diagnosis with source and severity.
Upper urinary infection plus several high-risk criteria.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sepsis from pyelonephritis**.

elim: Appendicitis gives RIF pain and a clean dipstick usually.
Ectopic gives pelvic pain, bleeding, no high fever with nitrites.
Renal colic is colicky pain without high fever unless infected.
Cystitis is lower urinary and does not cause shock.

steps.x: **D. Sepsis from pyelonephritis.** Infection + high-risk criteria.

practice.stem: A 71 year old man with a 2 day history of cough and fever is confused. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, BP 86/52 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Blood cultures have been taken and IV antibiotics given. The team want to assess how severe his tissue hypoperfusion is.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: Lactate is critical: a raised level shows hypoperfusion and its trend monitors resuscitation. Clinical diagnosis plus lactate is the gold standard.

steps.x: The test for hypoperfusion severity.

clues: how severe his tissue hypoperfusion is
steps.x: Sepsis already suspected; now quantify perfusion.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Lactate** (on a blood gas).

elim: CT is not first-line and does not measure perfusion.
D-dimer is non-specific in sepsis.
Procalcitonin marks bacterial infection, not perfusion.
Sputum culture finds the organism, not severity.

steps.x: **C. Lactate.** Clinical diagnosis plus lactate.

practice.stem: A 77 year old woman is treated for sepsis with IV antibiotics after blood cultures. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 110 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. She has no cough, abdominal pain or skin changes, and the source is unclear. She is incontinent of urine.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to identify the source?
practice.e: A full septic screen (urine culture, chest X-ray, sputum culture, imaging) finds the source; urine is the commonest source in older women.

steps.x: Second-line: find the source.

clues: no cough, abdominal pain or skin changes
steps.x: No chest, abdomen or skin source; urine is the likeliest.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Septic screen starting with **urine culture**.

elim: Bone scan is not part of a septic screen.
Echo only if endocarditis is suspected (murmur, positive cultures).
No meningism or headache.
Ferritin does not identify a source.

steps.x: **E. Urine culture.** Septic screen to find the source.

practice.stem: A 63 year old man has fever, confusion and a red, hot, swollen leg. His temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 126 bpm, BP 86/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air. Oxygen has been given, blood cultures taken, lactate measured and a 500 mL fluid bolus started.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
practice.e: Antibiotics are the single most important treatment and must be given IV within 1 hour. Waiting for cultures or tests delays life-saving therapy.

steps.x: What is still missing from the Sepsis Six?
Four of six done; antibiotics are not yet given.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV broad-spectrum antibiotics** within the hour.

elim: Imaging must not delay antibiotics.
Oral route is wrong in septic shock.
Never wait for cultures.
Cultures are already taken; swabbing must not delay treatment.

steps.x: **B. IV antibiotics now.** The most important part of the bundle.

practice.stem: A 69 year old woman with sepsis from a urinary source has received IV antibiotics and 2 L of 0.9% saline in boluses. Her pulse rate is 122 bpm, BP 80/44 mmHg (mean arterial pressure 56 mmHg) and urine output 10 mL per hour. Her chest is clear and her lactate is 4.8 mmol/L.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: Persistent hypotension despite fluids (septic shock) needs a noradrenaline infusion via ICU. Furosemide would worsen hypotension.

steps.x: Next step after fluids have failed.
Septic shock: MAP under 65 despite fluid.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **ICU for noradrenaline**.

elim: Diuretics drop BP further.
Oral midodrine has no role in acute septic shock.
A blood count does not treat shock.
She is far too unwell for oral antibiotics.

steps.x: **A. Noradrenaline via ICU.** Fluids fail = vasopressor.

practice.stem: A 56 year old man on haemodialysis via a tunnelled central line has fever and rigors starting during dialysis. His temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. The line exit site is red with pus. Blood cultures from the line and a peripheral vein grow Staphylococcus aureus. He has started IV antibiotics.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate additional management?
o: Continue the line and recheck in 1 week
practice.e: Source control means removing infected devices or lines and draining abscesses. Antibiotics alone rarely clear an infected line.

steps.x: What else besides antibiotics?

clues: exit site is red with pus
steps.x: The line is the source.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Source control: remove the line**.

elim: Adding an oral drug does not remove the source.
Flushing pushes more bacteria into the blood.
Leaving an infected line in risks persistent bacteraemia.
Steroids are not indicated; he is not in refractory shock.

steps.x: **D. Remove the line.** Source control.

practice.stem: A 72 year old woman with sepsis from pneumonia has warm peripheries and a bounding pulse. Her pulse rate is 124 bpm and BP 84/40 mmHg. Her BP does not improve after 2 L of IV fluid, and she develops oedema of her arms and legs.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her hypotension?
o: Loss of sympathetic tone from spinal injury
practice.e: TNF-alpha and IL-6 cause widespread vasodilation (warm, bounding) and capillary leak (oedema), giving relative hypovolaemia that fluids cannot fix.

steps.x: Mechanism of septic hypotension.

clues: warm peripheries and a bounding pulse
oedema of her arms and legs
steps.x: Low diastolic, warm and leaky: vasodilation plus capillary leak.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Cytokine-mediated vasodilation and capillary leak**.

elim: No bleeding; haemorrhage gives cold peripheries.
That is anaphylaxis; no allergen.
That is neurogenic shock; no spinal injury.
LV failure gives cold peripheries and pulmonary oedema.

steps.x: **B. Vasodilation and capillary leak.** The reason vasopressors are needed.

glossary.Sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.
glossary.Septic shock: Sepsis with persistent hypotension and low urine output despite adequate fluids, needing vasopressors.
glossary.Sepsis Six: Bundle completed within 1 hour: oxygen, blood cultures, IV antibiotics, IV fluids, lactate, urine output.
glossary.Lactate: Product of anaerobic metabolism; a raised level shows tissue hypoperfusion.
glossary.Hypoperfusion: Not enough blood flow to deliver oxygen to tissues.
glossary.Anaerobic metabolism: Energy production without oxygen, making lactate as a by-product.
glossary.MAP: Mean arterial pressure; under 65 mmHg is a high-risk sepsis criterion and the vasopressor target.
glossary.Vasopressor: Drug that constricts blood vessels to raise blood pressure.
glossary.Noradrenaline: First-line vasopressor for septic shock, given by infusion in ICU.
glossary.Vasopressin: Hormone used as a second vasopressor when noradrenaline alone is not enough.
glossary.Crystalloid: Clear salt-based IV fluid such as 0.9% sodium chloride.
glossary.Fluid bolus: A quick set volume of IV fluid (e.g. 500 mL) given to test and treat low blood pressure.
glossary.Piperacillin-tazobactam: Broad-spectrum IV penicillin with a beta-lactamase inhibitor; covers Gram-positive, Gram-negative and anaerobic bacteria.
glossary.Broad-spectrum: An antibiotic or regimen covering many types of bacteria before the organism is known.
glossary.Blood cultures: Blood bottles incubated to grow and identify bacteria in the bloodstream.
glossary.Septic screen: Set of tests to find the infection source: urine and sputum cultures, chest X-ray, imaging.
glossary.Source control: Removing the source of infection, e.g. draining an abscess or removing an infected line.
glossary.Cytokine: Signalling protein from immune cells; TNF-alpha and IL-6 drive sepsis.
glossary.TNF-alpha: Tumour necrosis factor alpha: a key pro-inflammatory cytokine causing fever and vasodilation.
glossary.IL-6: Interleukin 6: a pro-inflammatory cytokine that also drives the liver's acute-phase response.
glossary.Vasodilation: Widening of blood vessels, lowering blood pressure.
glossary.Capillary leak: Fluid escaping from damaged small vessels into tissues, causing oedema.
glossary.Acute-phase response: Liver shift towards making inflammatory proteins such as CRP during illness.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein: an acute-phase protein that rises in infection and inflammation.
glossary.Albumin: Main blood protein made by the liver; falls in sepsis.
glossary.Myocardial depression: Reduced pumping strength of the heart caused by inflammatory mediators.
glossary.Rigors: Violent shaking with a rapidly rising temperature, typical of bacteraemia.
glossary.Hypothermia: Body temperature below 36°C; can be how sepsis presents in older people.
glossary.Immunosuppression: Weakened immune system, e.g. from steroids, chemotherapy or methotrexate.
glossary.ABCDE: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure: the structured approach to an acutely ill patient.
glossary.Non-rebreathe mask: Oxygen mask with a reservoir bag delivering high-concentration oxygen at 15 L/min.
glossary.ICU: Intensive care unit, where vasopressors and organ support are given.
glossary.Pyelonephritis: Infection of the kidney, causing fever, loin pain and rigors.
glossary.NEWS2: National Early Warning Score: a UK score from observations used to spot deteriorating patients.
glossary.Oliguria: Low urine output, under about 0.5 mL/kg per hour.
glossary.Cholangitis: Infection of the bile ducts, usually from obstruction.
